## The Impossible Relay: Why Young People Don't Want to Be Bell Ringers

In Almuñécar, the generational relay of manual bell ringing has not broken down for lack of trying. It has worn away due to a combination of factors ranging from economic precariousness to a social perception that associates the trade with a bygone era. The local brotherhoods have organized workshops for teenagers in recent years, hoping to spark vocations among those who have not yet turned sixteen. The results have been meager: some youngsters show up out of curiosity, learn the first beats of the peal, but rarely return to the bell tower once they discover there is no paycheck at the end of the month.

Manual bell ringing requires a combination of physical dexterity, aural sensitivity, and traditional knowledge that cannot be acquired in a single afternoon. It is not enough to just pull the rope; one must understand the rhythms, the pauses, the nuances that distinguish a funeral toll from a festive peal. This knowledge is passed down from master to apprentice, in hours of practice that are not recorded in any contract. For a young person seeking career guidance, the equation is discouraging: months of training for a trade that doesn't pay the bills and receives little public recognition beyond the patron saint festivals.

The lack of remuneration is the first wall. In Almuñécar, traditional bell ringers have carried out their work voluntarily or in exchange for small symbolic gratuities that fall short of making it a job. The brotherhoods do not have the budget to hire apprentices, and local administrations have not allocated a specific fund to keep this practice alive. A teenager who compares the time invested in the bell tower with any summer job in the hospitality sector—a thriving industry on the Granada coast—finds few reasons to choose the rope over the bar of a beach bar.

The low social prestige exacerbates the situation. In a town focused on tourism and the modernization of its image, the bell ringer appears as a figure from the past, almost folkloric, that does not fit into the aspirational references of the youth. The workshops organized by the brotherhoods have run up against this invisible barrier: the boys participate with a mixture of curiosity and condescension, like someone attending a demonstration of an ancient craft in a living museum. They do not see a future in the bell tower, but rather a postcard.

The comparison with Villavante, where manual bell ringing has achieved a certain continuity, reveals a structural difference. There, the tradition has been integrated into a community calendar that gives it meaning and collective pride; in Almuñécar, manual bell ringing competes with a leisure and consumer offering that leaves no room for activities without immediate returns. The young people of Almuñécar do not reject the tradition out of contempt, but out of a pragmatic logic they have been taught since school: time is money, and the bell tower doesn't pay dividends.

The phrase from Villavante, recorded in the context of the heritage file, resonates here with a double reading. "AI will never be able to perform manual bell ringing" is a defense of the human factor, but also a realization that this human factor is dying out for lack of a relay. Artificial intelligence can program tolls, automate peals, and simulate rhythms, but it cannot replace the sensitivity of hands that interpret the wind, the rain, or the mood of the town. The problem is that those hands no longer find anyone to inherit them.

In Almuñécar, the last active manual bell ringer—whose identity the brotherhoods prefer not to expose publicly—has expressed in internal meetings his fear that the trade will die with him. There is no formal apprentice, no transmission protocol, and no municipal plan to guarantee continuity. The occasional workshops have served to document the practice, to record and archive it, but not to create a living chain of transmission. The difference between archiving and transmitting is the same as that between preserving a musical score and training a musician.

The paradox is that Almuñécar boasts of its historical heritage—the Castle of San Miguel, the salted fish factory, the Roman aqueduct—while letting a sonic heritage die, one that requires no architectural restoration, but rather political and social will. A silent bell tower is an incomplete monument, a voice fading away with no one to claim it. The bells are still there, hanging in their yokes, waiting for hands that are no longer coming.

The brotherhoods' attempts to attract teenagers have stumbled upon a methodological problem. The workshops have been set up as extracurricular activities, with no continuity or follow-up, and without a reference figure to act as a long-term mentor. A fourteen-year-old boy might get excited by his first peal, but that enthusiasm fades if there is no clear path, tangible recognition, or a community to embrace him. Learning manual bell ringing is not just another hobby; it is an initiation that requires time, patience, and an emotional bond with the place.

The lack of remuneration is not just an economic issue, but a symbolic one. Paying for manual bell ringing would mean recognizing that this knowledge has value, that it is not a grandfather's pastime or an ethnographic curiosity. As long as the bell ringer remains a voluntary figure, the implicit message is that their work does not deserve compensation, and that message sinks in with young people more forcefully than any heritage discourse. In Villavante, continuity has been sustained by a community network that values the ringing as part of its identity; in Almuñécar, that network has been weakened by tourist pressure and social fragmentation.

The impossible relay is not, therefore, a biological fatality. It is the result of decisions that have not been made, budgets that have not been allocated, and a perspective that continues to see the bell tower as a backdrop rather than a living organ of the social body. Young people are not fleeing manual bell ringing out of laziness or ignorance; they are fleeing a trade that no one has known how to make desirable. And without desire, there is no possible transmission.
